assessments.explanation: The court reviews the Refugee Protection Division's decision dismissing Mr. Mercado's refugee claim.
The court states it cannot agree with the applicant's attempt to raise new issues and dismisses the application.
The paragraph provides Mr. Mercado's personal background and his claim of fearing persecution in Venezuela.
Mr. Mercado describes his return to Venezuela, his work, and discovery of blacklists targeting his family.
He details the threats, harassment, and persecution he claims to have suffered in Venezuela.
Mr. Mercado states he left Venezuela after consulting a lawyer and traveling through Colombia and Mexico to the US.
He testifies about the timing and nature of his injuries and his inability to report to police due to threats.
The paragraph discusses the passports and identity documents of Mr. Mercado and his family members.
Documents including a driver’s license and medical report are filed with the immigration file.
Counsel files a lawyer’s letter and a work identity card during the hearing.
The applicant claims uncertainty about hearing details affected his preparation and evidence submission.
The paragraph details the notices of hearing and logistical issues faced by the applicant.
Mr. Mercado states he did not have the original work card in Canada as it was in Venezuela.
He requested more time to submit evidence, but the request was denied, and the decision was made the next day.
The RPD dismissed the claim, citing contradictions and inconsistencies in the evidence, including the driver’s license and medical report.
The court notes the contradictions are central to the applicant’s story and do not require further discussion.
The applicant argues the RPD erred in its reasoning regarding the absence of documents confirming his employment.
He claims the RPD violated natural justice by refusing to grant additional time to submit evidence.
The applicant argues the RPD imposed an unfair burden and judged him more harshly due to legal representation.
He contends he should have been informed earlier of the RPD’s doubts about his credibility and evidence.
The court notes the legal standards for reviewing credibility assessments and procedural fairness issues.
The reasonableness standard applies to credibility and evidence evaluation, citing relevant case law.
Procedural fairness breaches are reviewed under the correctness standard, citing relevant jurisprudence.
The court finds the RPD properly considered the evidence, despite the applicant’s claims to the contrary.
The ambiguity in paragraph 12 is due to literal interpretation, but the reasoning was sufficiently developed.
The court finds the RPD’s assessment of the evidence’s probative value was reasonable.
The applicant failed to submit the original work card and only provided a late, poor-quality copy.
The applicant had ample time and opportunity to gather supporting documents but did not do so.
The lawyer’s letter does not substantiate the key element of persecution, and the document lacks credibility.
The RPD reasonably expected the applicant to produce documents proving his presence and employment in Venezuela.
The medical report is outdated and does not mention the attack or hospital visit, weakening its evidentiary value.
Failure to submit supporting documents can impact credibility, especially when the applicant has not provided independent proof.
The RPD’s evaluation of the evidence was within reason and legally defensible.
The court considers whether the RPD breached procedural fairness based on the applicant’s arguments and evidence.
The RPD’s rules regarding evidence submission and discretion are examined for compliance with procedural fairness.
The RPD denied the applicant’s request for more time, citing lack of effort and undermining credibility.
The court finds the RPD properly applied the rules and considered the applicant’s efforts and explanations.
The RPD reasonably considered the applicant’s education, counsel, and the probative value of the evidence.
The presence of counsel was a relevant factor in assessing the applicant’s knowledge of filing requirements.
The RPD reasonably concluded the applicant had sufficient time and access to documentation in Venezuela.
The court finds no breach of procedural fairness as the applicant did not explain the unavailability of documents and the RPD's refusal was justified.
The court agrees that the RPD did not err in refusing to grant more time for the hearing.
The court clarifies that the driver’s licence issue is unrelated to the request for additional time and was not supported by new evidence.
The court notes that this paragraph introduces the last key question in the case.
The court considers whether new factors can be evaluated to determine if there was a denial of justice and if the RPD breached rights by not timely addressing doubts.
The court reports that counsel knew or should have known about the missing screening form before the hearing, referencing relevant case law.
The court finds that the failure to object timely was of little consequence because the form lacked impactful information, but this might differ in other cases.
The court summarizes the contents and date of the screening form and notes the RPD lacked certain documents at initial review.
The court explains that the applicant argued the credibility box should have been checked, but the court disagrees based on legal precedent.
The court states credibility is always key in refugee claims and the form's contents would not have changed the outcome, so no error is found.
The paragraph introduces the issue of the unsigned note in the applicant’s file.
The court finds it difficult to determine whether the note should have been raised earlier due to uncertainty about its origin and timing.
The court notes the applicant attributes the note to the RPO and that counsel obtained it before the hearing but cannot clarify its origin.
The court reviews the content of the note, which discusses inconsistencies in the applicant’s story and documents, noting the timing issues.
The court observes that the comments in the note are straightforward and could have been written by anyone reviewing the record.
The applicant did not cite jurisprudence supporting the need to be advised of the note’s contents, and his argument is unclear.
The applicant claims Rule 18 requires the RPD to notify claimants before using specialized information, which he argues was not done with the note.
The court states the applicant was informed of the RPD’s concerns at the hearing, so Rule 18’s application is limited here.
The court notes the RPD was not the source of the note and the authenticity of the driver’s licence was not challenged, making Rule 18 irrelevant.
The court concludes Rule 18 does not assist the applicant in this case due to lack of procedural violation.
The court states that if counsel received the document, concerns should have been raised with the RPD.
The court finds it implausible that the applicant and counsel were unaware of the inconsistency in the licence’s issuance date.
The applicant did not seek additional time to produce evidence about the Internet licence, so Rule 18 does not apply retroactively, and common sense suffices.
The court dismisses the application based on the previous reasoning.
The court notes no questions for certification and that the case depends on its facts.
